data.title: Singapore to unveil new maritime master plan in April 2027
data.description:
It will focus on port capacity, technology adoption, and workforce development.

Singapore will launch its next Maritime Singapore Master Plan in April 2027, Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow announced on 20 November.

Speaking at the Tuas Port Phase 2 groundbreaking ceremony, Siow said the plan will focus on expanding capacity across the port and maritime ecosystem, leveraging technology and innovation, and investing in workers.

“In the past year, the government has been engaging businesses, industry associations, unions, workers and youths to develop our next Maritime Singapore Master Plan,” he added.

Siow said Singapore plans to attract more global and regional headquarters of maritime companies, including those involved in ship financing, insurance, and data services.

The government also wants more commercial decisions and transactions supporting global shipping to be conducted from Singapore, including those involving supply-chain management and global operations.

Siow said port expansion will form part of this strategy.

Tuas Port's Finger Three, which spans nearly 400 hectares of reclaimed land, is expected to begin operations in 2028, with 21 deepwater berths operational by the mid-2030s.

The completed port is expected to handle 65 million twenty-foot equivalent units annually by the 2040s, he added.

On technology adoption, PSA International plans to expand its fleet to around 1,000 next-generation Intelligent Guided Vehicles.

Singapore also plans to integrate artificial intelligence, digital twins, autonomous systems, and real-time data to improve coordination across port operations.

The government is also expanding liquefied natural gas (LNG) bunkering, licensing suppliers for LNG and methanol, and conducting trials and developing safety standards for alternative fuels such as ammonia.

The third priority will focus on workforce development as port operations become increasingly automated.

“As PSA shifted towards more automation, Muadz upskilled to master our new automated systems at Tuas by completing a Work-Study Diploma in Port Automation, sponsored by PSA,” Siow added.

data.title: DBS new retail multi-asset fund raises $200m in two weeks
data.description:
Retail investors can make an initial investment from S$1,000.

DBS has launched the DBS CIO Barbell Strategy Fund, a multi-asset fund for retail investors.

The fund raised over S$200m (about US$155.02m) in its two-week initial offer period, and remains open for subscription via the DBS digital bank app.

Retail investors can make an initial investment from S$1,000 (US$775), with regular savings plans available from S$100 (US$77.5) per month.

The fund is guided by the Barbell Strategy of DBS’s chief investment office (CIO), which delivered a cumulative net return of 72.8% (7.9% annualised) from its inception in 2019 to 31 October 2026.

This is higher than the 45% (5.4% annualised) return of a reference index comprising equal weights of global equities and global bonds, DBS said.

The fund is managed by DBS’ discretionary portfolio management (DPM) team, and is actively allocated and rebalanced in line with the CIO’s house view and changing market conditions, the bank said.

(US$1 = S$1.29, as of 23 November 2026)

data.title: UOB signs MOU with Guangzhou for proposed technology centre
data.description:
UOB and the Guangzhou Municipal Government will work towards the next phase of planning and assessment.

UOB has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Guangzhou Municipal Government to establish a technology innovation centre in Guangzhou, China.

The proposed center is expected to add engineering capacity and specialist expertise to the bank, UOB said in an announcement on 20 November 2026. Strategy, architecture, and critical capabilities will remain anchored in Singapore.

UOB will also explore partnerships with universities, research institutions, and technology companies in Guangzhou and the Greater Bay Area to deepen access to talent, emerging technologies, and industry-academia collaboration.

“The centre will tap Guangzhou’s technology ecosystem to complement UOB’s regional capabilities, strengthening our ability to innovate and scale solutions across the Group as we advance our multi-year technology transformation,” said Lawrence Goh, head of group technology and operation at UOB.

Under the MoU, UOB and the Guangzhou Municipal Government will work towards the next phase of planning and assessment, with further details to be announced when finalised.

UOB has operated in mainland China for over four decades, first establishing representative offices and branches in Beijing in 1984 and Guangzhou in 1989. It incorporated a subsidiary in 2007.

data.title: China FTA upgrade talks to cover digital economy: PM Wong
data.description:
Other key cooperation areas include green development and connectivity.

Singapore and China have launched negotiations to upgrade their bilateral Free Trade Agreement (FTA), with plans to cover the digital economy and facilitate cross-border data flows. 

The proposed upgrade is expected to open up new opportunities for firms operating across both markets, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, following his bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping after the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

Both leaders discussed deepening cooperation in emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, he added.

The two countries are also expanding cooperation into areas such as green development and connectivity under their All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership.

Separately, Singapore and China are exploring closer trade links between western China and Southeast Asia through the newly opened Pinglu Canal and the International Land-Sea Trade Corridor.

The proposal was discussed during a meeting between Wong and Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing on 21 November.

data.title: Singapore, China eye closer trade links through Pinglu Canal
data.description:
Both sides explore synergies between major transport routes to support regional trade.

Singapore and China are exploring closer trade links between western China and Southeast Asia through the newly opened Pinglu Canal and the International Land-Sea Trade Corridor (ILSTC).

The proposal was discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing on 21 November, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) said.

Both countries will explore synergies between the ILSTC and China's Pinglu Canal under the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative to strengthen regional connectivity, economic integration and supply-chain resilience.

In a Facebook post, Wong said Singapore and China were building on their existing government-to-government projects to explore new opportunities, including closer connectivity between western China and Southeast Asia.

The two leaders also welcomed progress under their three government-to-government projects in Suzhou, Tianjin, and Chongqing, and agreed to adapt these initiatives to evolving priorities.

Under the Tianjin Eco-City project, Singapore and China will explore cooperation in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.

The MFA said Wong and Li reaffirmed their shared interest in maintaining an open and economically integrated region, including the importance of international law and freedom of passage in international waterways.

Both leaders also discussed closer cooperation during Singapore's ASEAN Chairmanship in 2027, particularly in regional connectivity, energy security and combating transnational scams.

They also welcomed opportunities to strengthen economic cooperation between ASEAN and China through the ASEAN-China Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade, the MFA added.

data.title: Firms prioritise workflow redesign and ownership to scale AI
data.description:
Executives cite business accountability and governance as key priorities. 

Businesses are prioritising workflow redesign and business ownership to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into daily operations and scale adoption, executives said at the Singapore Business Review Technology Enterprise Summit.

Jayant Raman, head of AI partnerships for Asia Pacific at Oliver Wyman, said that whilst large enterprises have developed AI pilots, few have successfully scaled them across their organisations.

Speaking as moderator of a panel discussion at the summit, Raman raised questions about how companies can move beyond experimentation to deliver business value whilst maintaining trust and governance.

James Fong, senior vice president of Enterprise Digital Ecosystem & Business at Changi Airport Group, identified four factors to consider before scaling AI initiatives: a genuine business problem, an accountable owner, economic value, and governance.

“I always remind my team not to let technology look for a problem to solve. First, we need to make sure there is a problem that needs solving,” he said in a panel discussion.

Fong added that businesses must assess whether the cost of deploying technology is justified by the value of the problem being addressed.

Abdel Abatouy, chief technology and information officer for Asia at FCM Travel, said companies should evaluate AI investments based on actual business outcomes rather than increases in output.

Abatouy said FCM had introduced agentic AI into its corporate travel booking workflows, allowing consultants to review recommended travel options based on customers' policies and preferences.

He said the system reduced the time needed to prepare customer quotes from six to eight hours to approximately 30 minutes.

The company also uses its Sam AI travel assistant to help manage travel disruptions, including identifying alternative arrangements when flights are cancelled. 

Rather than reducing headcount, FCM redeployed travel consultants to handle more complex travel requests and VIP services, which Abatouy said could generate additional revenue. The company also reported a significant reduction in employee overtime in Japan.

Meanwhile, Raymond Liu, Group Chief Transformation Officer at the National University Health System, said an AI pilot was conducted to summarise patient information before doctors' ward rounds.

Although the pilot demonstrated that the technology worked, it remained not fully scaled roughly 18 months later.

Liu attributed the delay partly to established clinical practices and resistance to changes in existing workflows. For example, junior doctors worried that arriving later than their colleagues because they had saved time using AI would reflect poorly on them.

Deskilling was also often seen as a problem.  "Are the junior doctors losing that ability to analyse and triage that information themselves?" Liu said, citing concerns about the potential loss of clinical assessment skills. 

Mohit Tandon, head of the Strategic Delivery Office, Tech&Ops at Prudential plc, said measuring the financial contribution of AI remains difficult because the technology is often embedded within broader business processes.

"It's more of an art than a science," Tandon said, noting the difficulty of attributing AI-related improvements directly to profit and loss.

He also warned that deploying AI without clearly defined objectives could increase workloads, particularly when managers must review low-quality AI-generated content.

“Without effective oversight & deployment, AI risks creating more work than it eliminates, as staff may spend time correcting or re-working AI-generated outputs, ultimately eroding the productivity gains it promises,” he said.

On governance, Tandon said organisations should distinguish between lower-risk applications, such as extracting information from medical documents, and higher-risk activities, such as making decisions on insurance claims.

"But you cannot also let autonomous agents take decisions on everybody's behalf," he noted, stressing that governance requirements should be proportionate to the risks involved.

Furthermore, the panellists discussed whether AI transformation should be managed centrally or by individual business units.

Abatouy said FCM had embedded AI champions across business units to complement its centralised centre of excellence, ensuring AI initiatives remain closely aligned with operational needs and business priorities.

"AI is owned by the business. It's owned by the CEO. It's the one driving it," he said.

For healthcare, Liu said central funding may be necessary when the benefits of AI investments accrue primarily to patients rather than the departments responsible for implementation.

He cited earlier lung cancer detection as an example of an application that could deliver significant patient benefits without necessarily generating corresponding financial returns for healthcare institutions.

data.title: Salary gaps challenge employers heading into 2027
data.description:
Reeracoen expects selective pay investment as employers balance recruitment budgets with workers’ expectations.

Employers face a mismatch between salary expectations and recruitment budgets heading into 2027, with 80.3% of hiring managers identifying pay expectations as a hiring challenge, according to Reeracoen.

The recruitment firm’s Singapore Salary & Hiring Guide 2026/2027 expects companies to remain selective, concentrating compensation spending on business-critical roles and capabilities that are harder to recruit.

Its research involving 375 Singapore hiring managers highlights the pressure employers face when competing for talent.

Separate employee research involving 337 respondents found that 47.5% considered base salary the single most important factor when choosing a job. Another finding showed that 58.8% would consider changing jobs for higher pay.

Reeracoen said employers needed to identify where uncompetitive compensation was restricting recruitment and where other elements of an offer could influence candidates’ decisions.

The guide pointed to improving hiring sentiment alongside continued caution over wage increases.

In July 2026, 48.7% of firms planned to hire over the following three months, whilst 27.9% expected to raise wages, according to Ministry of Manpower data cited in the report.

These figures describe near-term expectations in 2026 rather than confirmed plans for 2027.

Reeracoen’s employer watchlist identifies five priorities for the coming year: targeted hiring, salary expectations, skills mismatches, AI and skills readiness, and retention beyond pay.

It recommended comparing salaries with external market benchmarks rather than relying solely on a company’s historical pay levels.

Employers should also distinguish skills required immediately from those employees can learn after joining, whilst allowing longer recruitment lead times for specialist engineering roles.

For compensation planning, the guide favoured differentiated spending based on a role’s importance and the scarcity of relevant skills rather than uniform increases.

It also recommended strengthening retention before seeking replacements for difficult-to-fill positions.

Whilst salary remains central to employment decisions, Reeracoen said flexibility, career progression, benefits and manager quality also influence whether employees stay.

The guide presents a selective hiring and compensation outlook but does not forecast a specific salary-growth rate for 2027.

data.title: Singapore signs seven agreements to strengthen air hub
data.description:
The partnerships expand opportunities for airline services and aviation training across several regions.

Singapore has signed three air services agreements and four training agreements to strengthen its international aviation links and support air travel growth.

The agreements were concluded on 18 and 19 November on the sidelines of the seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference in Montreal, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore said.

Singapore upgraded its air services agreements with Brazil and Türkiye and signed its first such agreement with El Salvador.

Under the updated Türkiye agreement, designated airlines from both countries can operate additional passenger services without restrictions on capacity or aircraft type.

The Brazil agreement further liberalises the air services framework, including cargo operations, and establishes a foundation for potential direct flights as economic activity and exchanges between the countries grow.

The agreement with El Salvador enables connectivity through codesharing on flights via third countries. It also provides the regulatory framework for direct services when commercial opportunities arise.

Singapore and El Salvador currently have no direct passenger services, and the announcement did not include any new direct routes.

CAAS also signed training agreements with the International Civil Aviation Organization, Colombia, Mozambique and the Kyrgyz Republic.

ICAO and the Singapore Aviation Academy will jointly develop a 4.5-day Leaders in Aviation programme for directors-general of civil aviation. It will cover governance, safety and security oversight, sustainability, organisational leadership and resilience.

The other partnerships will support training and professional development for aviation personnel in Latin America and the Caribbean, Central Asia and Africa.

CAAS Director-General Han Kok Juan said Singapore would continue pursuing air services liberalisation to create opportunities for airlines to expand operations and improve travel convenience.

He added that partnerships with ICAO and other states would equip aviation leaders to address emerging challenges and support growing demand.

data.title: Daily Markets Briefing: STI down 2.11%
data.description:
Not a single STI constituent closed in positive territory.

The Straits Times Index (STI) closed at 4,972.230, down 2.11% on Friday, 20 November at 5:21 p.m.

Every STI constituent ended the session flat or in the red, with Seatrium Ltd the biggest loser, down 8.77%, followed by SATS (down 5.29%) and Venture Manufacturing (down 3.32%).

data.title: Mobile wallets hit cross-border barriers despite interoperability push
data.description:
In Africa, users often need a new wallet and KYC verification when crossing borders.

Mobile wallet users in Africa still face restrictions when making payments outside their home countries, highlighting gaps in cross-border payment connectivity despite efforts to improve interoperability.

“If I am Kenyan and go across the border to Tanzania, I cannot use my wallet to make a payment,” said Alvin Okari, managing director for East Africa at Capital Pay International, at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November.

Users often have to register for a new wallet and undergo another know-your-customer (KYC) process when entering a different country. In some cases, wallet access is also tied to the duration of their visa.

He called for regulators to address mobile wallet mobility and enable cross-border merchant acquiring so consumers can use their existing accounts when travelling.

Across East Africa, central banks have mandated interoperability between payment service providers, whilst local switches such as Tanzania's TIPS and Rwanda's R-switch allow providers to connect with multiple banks through a single application programming interface (API).

However, Okari said connecting domestic payment networks is not enough if users cannot access them across borders.

He pointed to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) as a framework that could facilitate digital payments between African countries.

Syed Mohammad Kamal, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh, said wider digital payment adoption also depends on incentives for merchants and consumers.

Merchants may prefer cash because digital transactions involve merchant discount rates (MDR) and make business activity more visible to tax authorities.

“Merchants are comfortable receiving cash nowadays because they are not within the tax net and are not paying anything extra for the MDR,” Kamal said.

He called for stronger incentives to encourage merchants to accept digital payments, alongside greater regulatory enforcement of interoperability.

Kamal also highlighted remittance costs as a barrier to formal payment channels. Bangladesh offers a 2.5% incentive for overseas citizens sending money through official channels, although informal remittance providers remain competitors.

Meanwhile, Stanislav Skvirsky, CEO of payme, cited Uzbekistan's remote identification and open banking regulations as measures that helped expand digital financial services.

The country introduced remote identification in 2016, allowing customers to access financial services without visiting bank branches.

Open banking rules also enabled customers to connect cards from different banks to fintech applications.

Uzbekistan additionally introduced 1% cashback on payments made through digital channels, including cards and mobile wallets.
